standard.title: Cultural preservation and heritage
standard.description: the cultural obligations of First Nations Australians about significant heritage sites, including ancestral remains, material culture and artefacts, and the role of collaboration between First Nations Australians and other individuals and groups to ensure cultural preservation
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe the social organisation and cultural practices of early First Nations Australians, including funerary customs, and explain how cultural knowledge has been transmitted through oral traditions and expressive arts (AC9HH7K06). They have not yet examined cultural obligations about heritage sites specifically, or the role of collaboration and institutional frameworks in cultural preservation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the cultural obligations of First Nations Australians regarding significant heritage sites, ancestral remains, and material culture; describe how the Lake Mungo case illustrates issues of ownership, cultural protocols, and repatriation; and explain the role of collaboration between Traditional Owners, researchers, and institutions in cultural preservation, including world heritage frameworks.

nodes.label: Cultural obligations and ancestral remains
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what cultural obligations First Nations Australians hold regarding significant heritage sites and ancestral remains, and describe why the disturbance of ancestral remains is a serious breach of cultural protocol.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain that First Nations Australians hold cultural obligations to significant heritage sites and ancestral remains, and that any unauthorised disturbance of ancestral remains constitutes a serious breach of cultural protocol.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the cultural obligations of First Nations Australians regarding heritage sites, ancestral remains, and material culture — including that ancestral remains are the ancestors of contemporary First Nations Peoples and that cultural protocols govern their treatment. Describe why these obligations are not simply legal requirements but expressions of ongoing cultural, spiritual, and kinship relationships.
wider: Examine specific examples of cultural protocols governing access to heritage sites — who has authority to speak for a site, what consultation processes are required, and how these protocols interact with Australian heritage law.
Investigate the concept of Country in relation to heritage obligations — how the obligation to care for ancestral remains and sites flows from the relationship between people, Country, and ancestors.

Explore the distinction between 'heritage' as understood in Western conservation frameworks and 'living culture' as understood by First Nations Australians — examining why the two frameworks sometimes produce different priorities.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who frame heritage obligations in Western property or conservation terms will misread the Lake Mungo case in N2 — they will analyse it as a legal dispute rather than understanding what the cultural protocol stakes actually are, missing the central dynamic of the case.

response_modes.reason: Students often approach heritage through a Western property/conservation framework, missing the relational and spiritual dimensions of First Nations cultural obligations. The reasoning chain — ancestral remains are ancestors, ancestors are part of ongoing kinship and cultural relationships, therefore disturbance ruptures living relationships, not just archaeological records — needs to be made explicit to overcome the misconception that heritage obligations are simply about protecting old things.

success_criteria: Explains that ancestral remains are understood as ancestors of contemporary First Nations Peoples, not simply archaeological material.
Describes why unauthorised disturbance of ancestral remains is a serious breach of cultural protocol — not just a legal infringement.
Does not frame heritage obligations purely in Western conservation terms — recognises the relational and spiritual dimensions.

nodes.label: Lake Mungo — ownership, repatriation, and collaboration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how the Lake Mungo case illustrates the issues of ownership, cultural protocols, research, and repatriation that arise when ancestral remains are discovered, and explain the collaborative processes involved in resolving these issues.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the Lake Mungo case — what was found, why it is significant, and what issues it raised regarding ownership, cultural protocols, and repatriation.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the Lake Mungo case in detail — the discovery of Mungo Man and Mungo Lady, their archaeological significance (among the oldest human remains in Australia), the issues of ownership and cultural protocols they raised for the Mutthi Mutthi, Paakantji, and Ngiyampaa Peoples, and the eventual repatriation process. Explain how this case became a landmark in negotiating the relationship between scientific research and First Nations cultural obligations.
wider: Examine the timeline of the Lake Mungo repatriation — the discovery, the period of scientific study, the advocacy by Traditional Owners, and the eventual return — analysing what this timeline reveals about evolving relationships between research institutions and First Nations communities.

Investigate the broader debate about the repatriation of cultural heritage internationally — such as the Elgin Marbles, Benin Bronzes, or First Nations skeletal collections held in overseas museums — and how the Lake Mungo case connects to these global debates.

Explore how Australian law (e.g. NAGPRA equivalents, ATSIHP Act) governs the treatment and repatriation of First Nations ancestral remains, examining how this legal framework has evolved in response to community advocacy.

response_modes.reason: The Lake Mungo case is specific and significant, but students need broader context — other repatriation cases, other heritage debates — to understand it as an instance of a wider pattern rather than an isolated incident. Breadth across cases helps students see that the tensions between research access and cultural obligations recur across different sites, different communities, and different countries, and that the collaborative resolution model is not automatic but achieved.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Lake Mungo case is historically rich, ethically substantive, and directly relevant to contemporary debates. Advancing students can engage with the genuine tensions between scientific and cultural knowledge claims, the ethics of research involving human remains, and the evolving legal and institutional frameworks for cultural heritage. It also connects to the K08 Ancient unit (archaeological methods and heritage conservation), making it a productive cross-unit link.
success_criteria: Describes what was found at Lake Mungo and why the find is archaeologically and culturally significant.
Identifies the specific issues raised — ownership, cultural protocols, research access, repatriation — and explains why each matters.
Does not frame the case as a simple conflict between science and culture — recognises the collaborative resolution process.

nodes.label: Collaboration and institutional roles in preservation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the roles of multiple stakeholders — Traditional Owners, researchers, government bodies, and institutions — in cultural preservation, and describe how collaboration and world heritage frameworks support the protection of significant sites.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the roles of at least two stakeholders (e.g. Traditional Owners and research institutions, or government bodies and community groups) in cultural preservation, and identify one institutional mechanism (e.g. world heritage listing, national galleries and archives) that supports preservation.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the roles of Traditional Owners, researchers, national and state institutions (galleries, libraries, archives, museums, historical societies), and government bodies in cultural preservation. Explain how collaboration between these stakeholders — rather than any single authority — is required for effective preservation. Describe how world heritage listing (e.g. Budj Bim, Willandra Lakes, Uluru-Kata Tjuta, Kakadu) functions as a mechanism for international recognition and protection.
wider: Examine the world heritage criteria in detail — examining which criteria Budj Bim, Willandra Lakes, and Kakadu satisfy, and what this reveals about how international frameworks assess the significance of First Nations cultural landscapes.

Investigate the roles and responsibilities of specific institutions — such as the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (AIATSIS) — in curating, repatriating, and making accessible First Nations cultural heritage.

Explore the tensions that can arise in collaborative heritage management — when Traditional Owner priorities, research interests, and tourism/access demands conflict — and how these are navigated through negotiated frameworks.

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the cultural obligations (Node 1) and the specific repatriation case (Node 2) into the descriptor's full demand: an understanding of how collaboration between First Nations Australians and other individuals and groups — including institutions and international bodies — functions to ensure cultural preservation. Students must coordinate the relational obligations, the specific example, and the institutional mechanisms into a coherent account.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two stakeholder groups and explains the role each plays in cultural preservation.
Describes at least one institutional mechanism (heritage listing, museum/archive role) and explains how it contributes to preservation.
Explains that effective preservation requires collaboration — not sole control by any single stakeholder.
